1: The first part was well answered with the most popular answers being growth, expansion and survival. Quite a number of candidates identified the business in the case as a new business and that, as such, survival was very relevant. Other good answers linked expansion to economies of scale and falling average costs but quite a few explanations went straight on to say that this would raise profit without explaining how it would happen, thus not providing adequate explanation for further credit. Only a very few candidates misread the rubric and offered profit as an objective. Part (b) was again well answered. Most answers which gained Level 2 marks were through a comparison of liabilities, control, sources of finance, level of risk, continuity or legal identity between a partnership and a private limited company. Disagreement between brothers/partners was common as was ease of setting up the business and the issuing of shares, then only Level 1 was achieved. Few candidates addressed the problems related to the planned expenditure and the consequent need to borrow and get the business established. There were quite a few candidates who muddled up limited and unlimited liability by name but not by content. Weaker candidates misunderstood public limited companies and private limited companies and some believed that selling shares increased profits. 2: Stronger candidates in part (a) usually explained interviews and questionnaires and sometimes consumer panels. Observation was occasionally given but not usually explained very well. Weak answers listed ringing people up or carrying out a survey. There was good reference to open and closed questions but the compulsion of those questioned to lie in their answers, was overestimated. Consideration of samples/sampling was not always clearly understood either, but overall the majority of candidates answered the question well and often gained at least 1 application mark. Candidates clearly knew about the three pieces of information in part (b) and consistently gained at least Level 1 marks with many also gaining Level 2. Sales forecasts were hardly ever linked to the anticipated figures in Appendix 1 but many candidates offered future profit and viability, with stronger candidates including the need to anticipate sales so as to idea and which site to buy. Cash flow forecasts were also well understood with many making reference to the seasonal nature of revenue. Application was predominantly for references to caravans and the brothers setting up a new campsite, but few candidates made very good use of the appendix/case study material. The most common error in part (b) was to confuse cash flow and profit. Only stronger candidates made clear why the information was important before setting up the campsite, hence gaining full marks.
3: This question had the weakest answers on the paper. Quite a number of candidates did not know what is meant by an external cost. Many knew that it was something to do with environmental degradation and could give examples, therefore gaining some marks but only the strongest candidates could offer answers relating to third party effects. The examples given by candidates usually related to animals and areas of beauty, noise, campfires, sewage, construction damage, deforestation and global warming. In part (b), calculations of break-even and net profit margin were fairly common. However, many candidates correctly calculated the first profit figure for site A, but then failed to adjust for lower occupancy in site B and site C. The cost of borrowing and the problem of getting government permission were frequently overlooked or ignored when making the final choice of which site to choose. This meant that answers which did not contain any calculations and just relied on qualitative comparisons, scored only low Level 2 marks. The most frequent error was with candidates approaching the choice from the consumers’ point of view, without then linking this to its effect on the firm’s sales/profits. For example, customers would find site A noisy but, even though occupancy figures suggested alternative views, these were often not included.
4: The first part was generally well answered with growth, employment, tax and currency appreciation being the most common responses, followed by explanations of how these outcomes would be generated. The commonest misconception was where candidates thought tourism would encourage investment from overseas, with no apparent reasoning/explanation apart from that visitors would see new opportunities and that tourists would then stay and take jobs in the country. Some useful answers were linked to import costs falling but these usually overlooked the impact on exports and visitors’ costs of travel. Part (b) showed that quite a number of candidates were unsure of how leasing worked and believed that the caravans could simply be returned at any time. A few weaker candidates thought the visitors would be leasing them. The main omission in several answers was to consider the costs involved if not all vans were rented. As the Appendix shows, two of the sites have less than 100% occupancy. Good answers considered that a new firm would find it difficult to borrow but may not want the commitment of leasing. Many stronger candidates correctly identified the benefits of asset ownership, depreciation, maintenance, and updating the vans. Quite a few candidates gave both or all options in their conclusion rather than answering the question and making a choice between the three options. Application marks were at least partially achieved by the majority of candidates.
5: The majority of candidates clearly knew the terminology and the correct stage names of the recruitment process, for example job analysis, job specification, advertising, interview and shortlist. Most candidates did not offer the answer in the logical order but no marks were lost as it was the stages which were required and not the correct order. Thankfully only a minority of answers offered job description, which was in the question and therefore not credited. The second part was quite well answered with virtually every candidate able to offer some Level 1 ideas - but the quality of the explanation was often lacking and did not go beyond Level 1. The idea that advertising on the Internet will directly lead to increased sales and profits was seldom evaluated. Better candidates linked the cost savings due to online booking, with attracting overseas visitors through the website, who can book beforehand and the owners receive payment before the customer arrives. Being able to check out the competition and plan accordingly was also a popular answer. Again, weaker candidates looked at the benefits from the customers’ perspective but then did not relate this to how the firm could, in turn, benefit from their happy campers - for example through loyalty, repeat bookings and favourable reviews.
